parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think on a microscopic scale - what particles are actually moving through a metal when a circuit is switched on?
parts.proper_answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge, or the movement/flow of charge carriers.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Charge In Motion**
Imagine sitting beside you and watching inside a copper wire. Current is not the wire itself moving, it is tiny charged particles - mainly free electrons in a metal - drifting along. So you need the idea of movement of charge.

Step 2: **State The Definition**
The examiner definition is simply: $$I = \frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta t}$$ in words, rate of flow of charge. Saying movement/flow of charge carriers earns the mark.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a volt measures - when charge moves between two points, what happens to electrical energy?
parts.proper_answer: p.d. is the work done, or energy transformed from electrical to other forms, per unit charge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy Per Charge Idea**
When charge flows through a lamp, electrical energy is lost as light and heat. Potential difference tells you how much energy is changed per coulomb that passes. It is an energy-per-charge quantity.

Step 2: **Give The Exact Definition**
In symbols: $$V = \frac{W}{Q}$$ In words: work done (or energy transformed) per unit charge. That phrase per unit charge is essential.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Start with Fig. 5.2 - for the circuit current of 0.30 A, read off the p.d. across one filament lamp.
Hint 2: Compare the total lamp p.d. for three lamps in series with the 8.7 V e.m.f. to find the p.d. left for the wires, then use V = IR for one wire.
parts.proper_answer: At $I = 0.30\text{ A}$, $V_{lamp} = 2.5\text{ V}$ from Fig. 5.2. Total for 3 lamps $= 7.5\text{ V}$. p.d. for 2 wires $= 8.7 - 7.5 = 1.2\text{ V}$, so $V_{wire} = 0.60\text{ V}$. $R = V/I = 0.60/0.30 = 2.0\,\Omega$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Voltage On One Lamp From The Graph**
You know the series current everywhere is $0.30\text{ A}$. Go to Fig. 5.2, find $I = 0.30\text{ A}$ on the vertical axis, read across to the curve and down. You get: $$V_{lamp} = 2.5\text{ V}$$ This is a common trap - do not assume lamps are ohmic, you must read the graph.

Step 2: **Use Conservation Of Energy Round The Loop**
Three identical lamps in series give: $$V_{lamps} = 3 \times 2.5 = 7.5\text{ V}$$ The supply provides $8.7\text{ V}$ with negligible internal resistance, so the missing voltage must be across the two connecting wires: $$V_{wires} = 8.7 - 7.5 = 1.2\text{ V}$$ Hence for one wire $V = 0.60\text{ V}$.

Step 3: **Apply V = IR To One Wire**
Each wire carries the same $0.30\text{ A}$: $$R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{0.60}{0.30} = 2.0\,\Omega$$ This shows the required result.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall how a metal wire at constant temperature differs from a filament lamp - what shape should its I-V graph have and where must it start?
Hint 2: Use your wire resistance of 2.0 ohm to work out the I/V gradient and think how steep it will look compared to the lamp curve on the same axes.
parts.proper_answer: Straight line through the origin with gradient $I/V = 1/R = 0.50\text{ A V}^{-1}$, much steeper than the lamp curve, e.g. passing through $(0.80\text{ V}, 0.40\text{ A})$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Ohmic Means Straight Line**
The question tells you resistivity does not vary with temperature, so the wire is ohmic and obeys $V = IR$ with constant $R$. Its $I$-$V$ graph is therefore a straight line through the origin: $$I = \left(\frac{1}{R}\right)V$$ Unlike the lamp curve which bends over due to heating, this stays linear.

Step 2: **Calculate The Gradient**
Gradient of $I$ against $V$ is: $$\text{gradient} = \frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{2.0} = 0.50\text{ A V}^{-1}$$ On Fig. 5.2 this is very steep. For example at the top of the graph $I = 0.40\text{ A}$, $V = IR = 0.80\text{ V}$. Draw a straight ruler line from (0,0) to about (0.8 V, 0.40 A), continuing - it will leave the top of the plotted area very quickly.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on one wire only - what current flows through it and what is its resistance from part (i)?
Hint 2: Choose the power formula that uses I and R directly and substitute with correct units to get watts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Select The Power Law**
Power dissipated as heat in a resistor can be written as $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$. Since you know $I$ and $R$ for the wire most directly, use: $$P = I^2R$$

Step 2: **Substitute Values**
For one wire $I = 0.30\text{ A}$ and $R = 2.0\,\Omega$: $$P = (0.30)^2 \times 2.0 = 0.09 \times 2.0 = 0.18\text{ W}$$ This is the wasted power loss in each connecting wire.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: List what you know for one wire - resistance 2.0 ohm, area 0.40 mm2, resistivity and electron density - and note mm2 must become m2.
Hint 2: Think how resistance links to material resistivity and dimensions to isolate the unknown length.
Hint 3: For drift speed, picture electrons drifting slowly through the wire cross-section - which quantities control how much current that drift creates?
Hint 4: Rearrange that current-drift relation to make v the subject and be careful with powers of ten and the elementary charge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Length From Resistivity**
Resistance depends on geometry by: $$R = \frac{\rho l}{A}$$ Rearranged for length: $$l = \frac{RA}{\rho}$$ Convert area: $0.40\text{ mm}^2 = 0.40 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$.

Step 2: **Calculate Length**
Substitute $R = 2.0\,\Omega$, $A = 0.40 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$, $\rho = 1.7 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{ m}$: $$l = \frac{2.0 \times 0.40 \times 10^{-6}}{1.7 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 47\text{ m}$$ The wires are surprisingly long, which is why their 2.0 ohm matters.

Step 3: **Recall The Drift Model**
Current is related to microscopic motion by: $$I = Anvq$$ where $A$ is cross-sectional area, $n$ is number density of free electrons, $v$ is drift speed and $q = e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ is electron charge. Drift speed is tiny because $n$ is huge.

Step 4: **Calculate Drift Speed**
Rearrange: $$v = \frac{I}{Anq}$$ $$v = \frac{0.30}{(0.40 \times 10^{-6}) \times (8.5 \times 10^{28}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19})}$$ Denominator $= 5.44 \times 10^{3}$, so: $$v \approx 5.5 \times 10^{-5}\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ That is only about 0.05 mm per second - electrons drift very slowly while the electrical signal travels near light speed.
